column3: A strict cafeteria: every fact sits in a tray with fixed labeled compartments; trays stack into tables, and no compartment may hold two foods.
column4: Data stored as relations: unordered tables of typed rows and named columns, addressed by value, never by position or pointer.
column5: CREATE TABLE users (id INT, name TEXT, city TEXT); / Each row is one fact: (7, 'Ada', 'London') / Rows have no inherent order; queries filter by value
column6: Spreadsheet — sheets address cells by position (B7); relations have no row order or cell coordinates, only values.

column3: A hotel front desk: every room has exactly one brass key with a number stamped in; no two rooms share a number, and a blank key with no number is refused.
column4: Column(s) that uniquely and non-nullably identify each row; every table should have exactly one.
column5: CREATE TABLE users ( / id BIGINT PRIMARY KEY, / email TEXT);
column6: UNIQUE constraint — UNIQUE allows NULLs and many per table; a PK is unique + NOT NULL and there is only one per table.

column3: A restaurant coat-check ticket #88 points to hook #88 in another room; the waiter (constraint) refuses to issue a ticket for a hook that doesn't exist — no orphan tickets.
column4: A column holding another table's primary key value, linking child rows to their parent row.
column5: CREATE TABLE orders ( / id BIGINT PRIMARY KEY, / user_id BIGINT REFERENCES users(id));
column6: Primary key — the PK lives in the parent and is unique; the FK lives in the child, may repeat, and may be NULL.

column3: A fishmonger works right to left: nets the whole lake (FROM), throws back the small fish (WHERE), then fillets only the cuts you ordered (SELECT).
column4: Core query shape: FROM picks tables, WHERE filters rows, SELECT projects columns — logically evaluated in that order.
column5: SELECT name, email / FROM users / WHERE created_at >= '2026-01-01';
column6: Written order vs logical order — you type SELECT first, but the engine runs FROM, then WHERE, then SELECT.

column3: A podium ceremony: all marathon finishers are lined up by time (ORDER BY), then only the first three climb the podium (LIMIT 3); everyone else goes home unlisted.
column4: ORDER BY sorts the result set; LIMIT (with OFFSET) caps how many of the sorted rows come back.
column5: SELECT name, seconds FROM runners / ORDER BY seconds ASC / LIMIT 3;
column6: GROUP BY — GROUP BY collapses rows into groups; ORDER BY only rearranges them, the row count is unchanged.

column3: You sort a coin heap into labeled jars, then weigh whole jars. You may report a jar's label or its weight — never one particular coin; it melted into the group.
column4: Collapses rows sharing key values into one row per group, so aggregates (COUNT, SUM, AVG) summarize each group.
column5: SELECT country, COUNT(*), AVG(age) / FROM users / GROUP BY country;
column6: DISTINCT — DISTINCT only dedupes rows; GROUP BY builds groups you can run aggregates over.

column3: WHERE is the bouncer screening individual coins at the door; HAVING is a second bouncer who weighs the finished jars and tips out any jar under 100 grams.
column4: Filters whole groups after aggregation, so its conditions can use aggregate results; WHERE cannot.
column5: SELECT country, COUNT(*) AS n / FROM users GROUP BY country / HAVING COUNT(*) > 100;
column6: WHERE — WHERE screens individual rows before grouping; HAVING screens completed groups after aggregation.

column3: A masked stranger at the party: asked 'are you Bob?' they shrug (UNKNOWN). Even two masked strangers side by side cannot confirm they are the same person.
column4: NULL means unknown: comparisons involving NULL yield UNKNOWN, so NULL = NULL is not true; test with IS NULL.
column5: SELECT NULL = NULL; -- NULL, not true / SELECT * FROM users WHERE email IS NULL; / WHERE x <> 5 also drops rows where x IS NULL
column6: Zero or empty string — those are known values; NULL is the absence of a value and poisons any comparison to UNKNOWN.

column3: Two families hand in wedding guest lists. UNION merges them and crosses out the duplicate cousin; UNION ALL seats her twice; INTERSECT keeps only names on both lists; EXCEPT strikes everyone the other family invited.
column4: UNION, INTERSECT and EXCEPT combine two queries' rows vertically; UNION dedupes unless you say UNION ALL.
column5: SELECT city FROM stores / UNION / SELECT city FROM suppliers; -- UNION ALL keeps dupes
column6: JOIN — joins glue columns side by side by matching keys; set ops stack rows from column-compatible queries.

column3: You tell the taxi driver 'the opera house', not turn-by-turn directions; the driver (query planner) knows tonight's traffic and picks the route. EXPLAIN is peeking over his shoulder.
column4: SQL states what result you want; the optimizer chooses how — access paths, join order, and algorithms.
column5: You write: SELECT * FROM users WHERE age > 30 / Planner decides: index scan vs seq scan, / join algorithm, table order
column6: Imperative code — loops spell out every step; declarative queries leave the steps to the planner.

column3: Speed dating night: only couples whose numbers match on both cards leave together into the results room; wallflowers without a match simply go home unrecorded.
column4: Pairs rows from two tables where the join condition matches; rows with no partner appear nowhere in the result.
column5: SELECT o.id, u.name / FROM orders o / JOIN users u ON u.id = o.user_id;
column6: LEFT JOIN — outer joins keep unmatched rows padded with NULLs; inner join silently drops them.

column3: A generous host: every guest from the left list gets a seat even without a date; the missing partners are cardboard cutouts labeled NULL. FULL OUTER seats both walls of wallflowers.
column4: LEFT, RIGHT and FULL joins keep unmatched rows from one or both sides, filling the missing columns with NULL.
column5: SELECT u.name, o.id / FROM users u LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.user_id = u.id; / -- users with no orders show o.id = NULL
column6: Inner join — inner returns only matched pairs; outer preserves the unmatched side(s) with NULL padding.

column3: The index at the back of a fat textbook: sorted terms with page numbers. You jump 'polymorphism -> p.412' instead of reading 900 pages; the book itself stays unsorted.
column4: A sorted side structure (usually a B-tree) mapping key values to row locations, turning full scans into O(log n) lookups.
column5: CREATE INDEX idx_users_email ON users(email); / SELECT * FROM users WHERE email='a@b.c' / -- descends 3-4 index pages, then fetches the row
column6: Primary key — a logical uniqueness rule (usually backed by an index); an index is the physical lookup structure itself.

column3: A phone book sorts by last name, then first. Finding 'Smith' or 'Smith, John' is instant; finding every 'John' regardless of surname means reading the entire book.
column4: An index on (a, b) serves filters on a, or on a and b — but not on b alone; column order decides usefulness.
column5: CREATE INDEX ON people (last_name, first_name); / WHERE last_name='Smith' AND first_name='John' -- uses it / WHERE first_name='John' -- cannot
column6: Two single-column indexes — separate indexes can't act as one sorted (a,b) structure; order within one index is what matters.

column3: The index card already has the whole answer written on its back — the librarian answers from the card drawer without ever walking to the filing cabinet.
column4: An index containing every column a query needs, so the engine answers from the index alone — an index-only scan, no table fetch.
column5: CREATE INDEX ON orders (user_id, status, total); / SELECT status, total FROM orders WHERE user_id = 7; / -- index-only scan: heap never touched
column6: Composite index — composite is about multiple key columns; covering means the query needs nothing beyond the index.

column3: Searching 'female patients' in a maternity ward — the index shrugs, nearly every row matches. Searching one passport number is a needle the index hands you instantly.
column4: The fraction of rows a predicate keeps; indexes shine when few rows match and lose to full scans when most rows do.
column5: WHERE passport_no='X99' -- 1 of 10M rows: index wins / WHERE active=true -- 80% of rows: / planner picks a seq scan; the index would thrash
column6: Cardinality — cardinality counts distinct values in a column; selectivity is the fraction of rows a specific filter passes.

column3: X-ray glasses for your query: put them on and its skeleton appears — a fat Seq Scan femur right where you swore an index lived.
column4: Shows the optimizer's chosen plan — scans, join order and algorithms, row estimates; the ANALYZE variant executes and adds real numbers.
column5: EXPLAIN ANALYZE SELECT * FROM orders WHERE user_id=7; / Seq Scan on orders (cost=0.00..4582 rows=98750) / -- no index used; estimates vs actuals visible
column6: EXPLAIN vs EXPLAIN ANALYZE — plain EXPLAIN only estimates; ANALYZE really runs the query and reports true times and row counts.

column3: An author with twelve secretaries: each sentence he writes, all twelve re-file cards in their own catalogs. A thirteenth catalog makes lookups snappier and his pen heavier.
column4: Every INSERT, UPDATE or DELETE must also maintain each index on the table, so each extra index slows every write.
column5: Table with 6 indexes: / one INSERT = 1 heap write + 6 index updates / Bulk-load trick: drop indexes, load, rebuild
column6: 'Indexes always help' — they help the reads that use them; every write pays for all of them whether used or not.

column3: A waiter takes a 30-guest table's order, then makes thirty separate sprints to the bar, one drink per trip, instead of one loaded tray. The kitchen is fine; the hallway is the bottleneck.
column4: Code fetches a list with one query, then loops issuing one query per item — N+1 round trips instead of one join or batched query.
column5: users = q('SELECT * FROM users') # 1 / for u in users: / q('SELECT * FROM orders WHERE user_id=%s', u.id) # +N
column6: Slow query from a missing index — each N+1 query may be fast; the killer is round-trip count, fixed by eager loading or IN-batching, not an index.

column3: Pairing socks three ways: hold each sock against every other (nested loop); toss them into color bins and match within bins (hash); or sort both piles and zip down them in step (merge).
column4: Engines match rows via nested loop (small or indexed inner), hash join (big unsorted inputs), or merge join (both inputs sorted).
column5: Nested loop: outer 10 rows, inner has index / Hash: build hash of small table, probe with big / Merge: both sorted on key, single zip pass
column6: Join types (INNER/LEFT) — types define which rows belong in the result; algorithms only define how the engine finds them.

column3: Marie Kondo for data: every fact gets exactly one drawer; a duplicated fact sparks no joy and is folded away into its own table, leaving a key behind as the receipt.
column4: Structuring tables so every fact is stored exactly once, removing redundancy by decomposing along functional dependencies.
column5: Instead of orders repeating user_name, user_addr: / users(id, name, addr) + orders(id, user_id) / Address change: 1 row, not 400
column6: Denormalization — the deliberate reverse: reintroducing duplication for read speed once you know the cost.

column3: The teacher's address is copied onto all 30 student cards. She moves and one card is missed (update); a teacher with no students can't be stored anywhere (insert); the last student leaves and her address is shredded with the card (delete).
column4: Redundancy breeds update anomalies (miss one copy), insert anomalies (fact needs a host row), and delete anomalies (fact dies with its row).
column5: employees(name, dept, dept_phone): / phone changes -> update 40 rows, miss 1 -> two truths / delete last employee -> dept phone vanishes
column6: Concurrency anomalies (dirty/phantom reads) — those come from parallel transactions; these come from redundant schema design.

column3: One egg per carton cup. Someone crammed three phone numbers into one cup; the lid won't close until each egg gets its own cup — or its own carton row.
column4: Every column holds one atomic value per row — no arrays, comma lists, or repeating groups; multi-values become extra rows.
column5: Bad: phones = '555-1, 555-2, 555-3' / Good: user_phones(user_id, phone) / one row per number
column6: 2NF — 1NF is about atomic cells; 2NF is about columns depending on the whole composite key.

column3: A safe that needs both keys (order_id + product_id) to open — yet 'product price' pops out with the product key alone. It never belonged in this safe; escort it to the products vault. The WHOLE key.
column4: 1NF plus no partial dependency: every non-key column must depend on the whole composite key, not just part of it.
column5: order_items(order_id, product_id, qty, product_name) / product_name depends on product_id alone -> partial / move it: products(product_id, product_name)
column6: 3NF — 2NF removes dependencies on part of the key; 3NF removes non-key columns depending on other non-key columns.

column3: A gossip chain: the row tells zip, zip tells city — city learned the key's secret secondhand. Cut out the middleman: zip and city elope to their own table. Nothing but the key, so help me Codd.
column4: 2NF plus no transitive dependency: non-key columns may not depend on other non-key columns — nothing but the key.
column5: people(id, zip, city): zip -> city is transitive / split: people(id, zip) + zips(zip, city) / city stored once per zip
column6: BCNF — BCNF additionally forbids non-candidate-key determinants even when the dependent column is part of a key.

column3: Bouncer-Codd at the club door: anyone caught determining anything ('this tutor fixes the course') must flash a full candidate-key membership card. Mere column cliques are thrown out and given their own venue.
column4: Stricter 3NF: every determinant (left side of any functional dependency) must be a candidate key — no exceptions.
column5: (student, course) -> tutor, but tutor -> course / tutor determines yet isn't a candidate key / decompose: tutors(tutor, course) + enroll(student, tutor)
column6: 3NF — 3NF tolerates a non-key determinant when the dependent is part of some key; BCNF tolerates nothing.

column3: The barista tapes the top ten recipes to the espresso machine instead of walking to the recipe book. Pours are instant — but when HQ changes the mocha, she must remember every taped copy or serve the old drink.
column4: Deliberately duplicating or precomputing data to cut joins and speed reads, accepting extra write logic and drift risk.
column5: orders.items_count kept by trigger / vs COUNT(*) join on every page load / faster read, one more thing to keep true
column6: Unnormalized design — denormalized is a measured step back from a normalized model; unnormalized never had one.

column3: A sheriff's star: the fat metal center is the fact table (every sale stamped with numbers), and each point of the star is a dimension — who bought, what item, which store, what day.
column4: Analytics layout: a central fact table of measured events joined to small denormalized dimension tables — who, what, when, where.
column5: fact_sales(date_id, store_id, product_id, qty, rev) / dim_date, dim_store, dim_product / query: join facts to a few dims, aggregate
column6: Snowflake schema — snowflake re-normalizes dimensions into sub-tables; star keeps each dimension flat and wide.

column3: The prison files inmates by number, not name: names get remarried, misspelled, and duplicated; number 24601 never changes no matter what Jean Valjean calls himself this year.
column4: Surrogate keys are meaningless generated IDs; natural keys are real-world attributes whose meaning can change, collide, or leak.
column5: id BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY -- surrogate / vs PRIMARY KEY (email) -- natural / email changes -> every referencing FK must change
column6: UUID vs auto-increment — both are surrogates; that choice is about generation and index locality, not business meaning.

column3: A furniture store that sells every chair as a bin of loose screws with sticky notes: 'color: red', 'legs: 4'. Infinitely flexible shelving — but rebuilding one chair takes forty trips, and nothing stops 'legs: banana'.
column4: Storing data as generic entity-attribute-value rows for 'flexibility', losing types, constraints, and sane queries in the bargain.
column5: attrs(entity_id, attr, value) / (42,'color','red'), (42,'legs','4') -- all TEXT / one product = N self-joins; no CHECK possible
column6: JSONB column — a typed, indexable document kept in one row; EAV shreds each attribute into its own untyped row.

column3: A magician's tablecloth yank: either the whole new table setting appears in one motion, or the trick fails and every plate is exactly where it was. The audience never sees half-moved cutlery.
column4: A group of statements executed as one all-or-nothing unit: COMMIT makes all of it visible; ROLLBACK erases every trace.
column5: BEGIN; / UPDATE acc SET bal=bal-100 WHERE id=1; / UPDATE acc SET bal=bal+100 WHERE id=2; COMMIT;
column6: Single autocommit statement — each statement is already its own tiny transaction; BEGIN binds several into one fate.

column3: Drop a committed transaction into a vat of acid: it stays in one piece (A), keeps its lawful shape (C), doesn't react with its vat-mates (I), and the etching it leaves is permanent (D).
column4: Atomicity (all or nothing), Consistency (rules still hold), Isolation (concurrent txns don't interfere), Durability (committed survives crashes).
column5: Crash between debit and credit -> both roll back (A) / CHECK bal >= 0 still true after (C) / power cut after COMMIT -> transfer survives (D)
column6: BASE — BASE systems trade per-transaction guarantees for availability, converging eventually instead of immediately.

column3: Reading a friend's essay over their shoulder mid-edit and quoting a sentence they delete a second later — your citation points at words that never made the published page.
column4: Reading another transaction's uncommitted changes; if it rolls back, you acted on data that never officially existed.
column5: T1: UPDATE acc SET bal=0 (not committed) / T2: SELECT bal -> 0, ships a refund / T1: ROLLBACK -- T2 refunded money that never moved
column6: Non-repeatable read — that one re-reads committed changes; a dirty read sees changes that were never committed at all.

column3: You check the hotel room price, walk off to fetch your wallet, and return to the same screen in the same session — the same room now costs more. Same row, same query, two answers.
column4: Within one transaction, re-reading the same row returns a different value because another transaction committed an update in between.
column5: T1: SELECT price WHERE id=7 -> 100 / T2: UPDATE price=120; COMMIT / T1: SELECT price WHERE id=7 -> 120 (same txn)
column6: Phantom read — phantom is new rows appearing in a re-run range query; non-repeatable is one existing row changing value.

column3: You count twelve ghosts in the ballroom, blink, count again: thirteen. None of the originals changed — a phantom matching your WHERE clause materialized between counts.
column4: Re-running a range query inside one transaction returns new rows that another transaction inserted and committed meanwhile.
column5: T1: SELECT COUNT(*) WHERE age>60 -> 12 / T2: INSERT senior; COMMIT / T1: same COUNT -> 13; a new row appeared
column6: Non-repeatable read — that is an existing row changing; phantom is the membership of the result set changing.

column3: Hotel privacy tiers: glass walls (neighbors see your dirty drafts), curtains (you see only finished rooms), a locked door (your view frozen at check-in), and a private floor where stays replay as if guests came one at a time.
column4: A ladder trading anomalies for concurrency: read uncommitted, read committed, repeatable read, serializable — each rung blocks more anomalies.
column5: SET TRANSACTION ISOLATION LEVEL REPEATABLE READ; / Postgres default: READ COMMITTED / serializable may abort: catch and retry
column6: Consistency (the C in ACID) — that is about domain rules holding; isolation is about what concurrent transactions can see.

column3: Two wiki editors type freely on the same page. On save, the site compares version numbers: first saver wins; the second sees 'page changed since you loaded it — reapply'. Nobody waited; one redid work.
column4: Proceed without locks; at write time verify a version or timestamp hasn't changed — if it has, abort and retry. Best when conflicts are rare.
column5: UPDATE docs SET body=:new, version=version+1 / WHERE id=7 AND version=:seen; / -- 0 rows updated => conflict: reload and retry
column6: Pessimistic locking — pessimism blocks rivals up front; optimism never blocks and detects conflicts at commit time.

column3: The office bathroom-key school of concurrency: take the key off the hook before you go; everyone else shuffles in the hallway, even those who only wanted to check the mirror.
column4: Acquire the lock before touching the data so no rival can modify (or lock) it until you finish; everyone else queues.
column5: BEGIN; / SELECT * FROM inventory WHERE sku='A1' FOR UPDATE; / -- rival writers block here until COMMIT
column6: Optimistic locking — optimism lets everyone work and rejects late writers; pessimism makes late arrivals wait at the door.

column3: You lay your flat hand on the bakery's last éclair while fishing out your wallet. Everyone may still look at it, but nobody can grab or reprice it until you finish paying (COMMIT).
column4: A row-locking read inside a transaction: locks the selected rows so your read-then-write sequence can't be interleaved by rivals.
column5: BEGIN; / SELECT bal FROM acc WHERE id=1 FOR UPDATE; / UPDATE acc SET bal=bal-100 WHERE id=1; COMMIT;
column6: Plain SELECT in a transaction — ordinary reads take no row locks; FOR UPDATE holds the rows until commit.

column3: Two overpolite people wedged in a doorway, each holding the door the other needs, bowing 'after you' forever — until the manager (the engine) shoves one back outside (abort) so the other passes; the ejected one retries.
column4: Two transactions each hold a lock the other needs, waiting forever; the database detects the cycle and aborts one as the victim.
column5: T1: locks row A, wants B / T2: locks row B, wants A / ERROR: deadlock detected -- fix: lock rows in same order
column6: Ordinary lock wait — blocking ends when the holder commits; a deadlock is a cycle only a victim abort can break. | cf. 530 Deadlock (déjà pris): same wait cycle, but the database detects it and kills one victim transaction automatically

column3: Across from the strict relational cafeteria, a food-truck park: each truck serves one dish its own way — no shared menu, no table service, no substitutions, and the lines fly.
column4: Non-relational stores that give up joins, strict schemas, or full ACID to win scale, flexibility, or speed for specific access patterns.
column5: Redis (key-value), MongoDB (document), / Cassandra (wide-column), Neo4j (graph) / pick per workload, not by fashion
column6: NewSQL — NewSQL keeps SQL and ACID while scaling out; NoSQL changes the data model itself.

column3: A wall of gym lockers: present exactly key #417 and get your bag. Ask the attendant 'which lockers contain red jackets?' and he just stares — lockers are opaque; only keys open anything.
column4: Stores an opaque value under a unique key; you can GET, SET, and DELETE by exact key but never query inside the value.
column5: SET session:abc '{user:7}' EX 3600 / GET session:abc -> '{user:7}' / -- no WHERE, no query by value
column6: Document store — documents are queryable and indexable by inner fields; a KV value is a sealed blob.

column3: Each customer is one manila folder: orders stapled inside, addresses paper-clipped to the flap. You pull the whole folder in one motion — no reassembling a person from ten separate drawers.
column4: Stores JSON-like documents with nested structure, indexed and queried by inner fields; the document is the unit of atomicity.
column5: db.users.find({'address.city': 'Oslo'}) / db.users.updateOne({_id:7}, {$push:{orders:o}}) / -- one document updated atomically
column6: Key-value store — KV can't see inside its values; a document DB indexes and filters on nested fields.

column3: A mile-wide spreadsheet where each row grows its own private set of labeled columns; the wall is sawn into panels by row key and the panels are shipped to different warehouses (partitions).
column4: Rows keyed by a partition key hold sparse dynamic columns sorted by a clustering key; built for huge, write-heavy, partitioned workloads.
column5: Cassandra: PRIMARY KEY ((user_id), ts) / partition by user, rows time-sorted inside / great: feeds, sensor series; bad: ad-hoc joins
column6: Columnar format (Parquet) — despite the name, wide-column stores are row-oriented per partition; columnar is a scan-optimized file layout.

column3: A detective's corkboard: photos (nodes) joined by red string (edges). 'Friend of a friend of a friend' is walking three strings with your finger — no re-sorting file cabinets (joins) at every hop.
column4: Nodes and edges are first-class records with direct pointers, so multi-hop relationship traversals stay fast regardless of dataset size.
column5: MATCH (a:Person {name:'Ada'})-[:FRIEND*2..2]->(f) / RETURN f.name / -- friends-of-friends in one traversal
column6: Join table in SQL — models the same edges, but each hop costs a join; graph engines follow stored pointers per hop.

column3: The alkaline answer to ACID: a spilled BASE spreads slowly across the lab counter until it evenly coats it (replicas converge eventually) — and the counter stays usable the whole time (available).
column4: Basically Available, Soft state, Eventually consistent: replicas may briefly disagree but converge; availability beats instant consistency.
column5: cart on two replicas briefly differs / partition heals -> versions reconcile / user never saw an error page
column6: ACID — ACID promises every transaction sees consistent data now; BASE promises the system converges later.

column3: A junk drawer you fill freely for years; sorting happens only at the moment a hand goes in. Each family member imposes a different order — batteries by size, or by 'probably dead'.
column4: Data is written without enforced structure; each reader applies a schema at query time, so interpretation is deferred and may vary.
column5: raw JSON logs land in S3, no table upfront / df = spark.read.schema(s).json('s3://logs/') / two teams read the same files differently
column6: Schemaless — data always has implicit structure; schema-on-read merely moves enforcement from write time to read time.

column3: The chef stocks each station for tonight's menu, not alphabetically: the garnish sits beside the plate it lands on. Orders (queries) fly out because the layout mirrors them; an off-menu request means re-prepping the kitchen.
column4: In NoSQL, model tables and keys from the exact queries you must serve — not from entity shape — because ad-hoc joins don't exist.
column5: DynamoDB: list the queries first: / 'orders by user by date' -> PK=user_id, SK=order_date / a new query pattern may need a new GSI/table
column6: Entity-relationship modeling — relational designs entities first and trusts joins for any query; NoSQL bakes the query into the layout.

column3: Scrapbooking: glue the photo onto the page (embed — instant to view, but a shared photo is re-printed onto every page) or write 'see album B, photo 12' (reference — one original, an extra walk to the shelf).
column4: Document modeling choice: nest related data inside the parent (one fast read, duplication) or store an ID to fetch separately (one copy, extra trip).
column5: Embed: {order:1, items:[{sku,qty}...]} one read / Reference: {order:1, item_ids:[9,12]} / + second query; items deduped across orders
column6: SQL foreign key — a document reference is app-resolved with no enforced integrity; an FK is engine-enforced and joinable.

column3: One hospital, many archives: X-ray films in the imaging vault, blood samples in the cold fridge, appointments in the front ledger. One patient, three purpose-built stores — and three systems for the night shift to keep alive.
column4: Using several database types in one system, each chosen for the workload it serves best, at the cost of operating them all.
column5: Postgres: orders and money / Redis: sessions; Elasticsearch: product search / S3: images -- one app, four stores
column6: Multi-model database — one engine exposing several models; polyglot runs separate specialized engines side by side.

column3: The fridge is downstairs, so your desk's top drawer holds the snacks you actually keep reaching for. The drawer is tiny — every new snack squeezed in shoves a neglected one out.
column4: A small fast store holding copies of hot data so repeat reads skip the slow source; effectiveness lives and dies by hit ratio.
column5: v = redis.get(k) # ~0.1 ms / if v is None: v = db.query(k) # ~5 ms / 99% hit ratio -> DB sees 1% of reads
column6: Memoization / CPU cache — same principle at other layers; this tier caches data between app and database (e.g. Redis).

column3: You open the snack drawer yourself; it's empty, so YOU trudge to the fridge and, walking back, drop a copy in the drawer for next time. The drawer never restocks itself — it's a dumb box.
column4: The app checks the cache first, on miss reads the database itself, then writes the result back into the cache; the cache stays passive.
column5: v = cache.get(k) / if v is None: / v = db.get(k); cache.set(k, v, ttl=300)
column6: Read-through — there the cache itself fetches from the source on a miss; in cache-aside the application does the fetching.

column3: A vending machine with a tiny stocker living inside: you only ever press the button. If the slot is empty, his arm reaches back into the warehouse, loads the slot, and the can drops — you never see the warehouse.
column4: The app only ever asks the cache; on a miss the cache itself loads the value from the backing store, returns it, and keeps it.
column5: cache = Caffeine.newBuilder() / .build(key -> db.load(key)); / v = cache.get(k) // miss handled inside
column6: Cache-aside — the app does the DB round trip there; read-through hides the source behind the cache API.

column3: A carbon-copy pad: one pen stroke writes the top sheet (cache) and presses through to the ledger page beneath (database) in the same motion. The stroke drags a little — but the sheets can never disagree.
column4: Writes go to the cache and synchronously to the backing store before acknowledging; never stale, but writes pay full latency.
column5: def put(k, v): / db.write(k, v) # sync / cache.set(k, v) # ack only after both
column6: Write-behind — behind acknowledges first and flushes later (fast, can lose data); through is synchronous and safe.

column3: The bartender chalks your rounds on a slate instantly and settles with the register in one batch at closing. Lightning service — but if a spilled beer wipes the slate before settling, those rounds never happened.
column4: Writes hit the cache and are acknowledged immediately, then flushed to the backing store asynchronously — fast, but a crash loses unflushed writes.
column5: cache.set(k, v); ack() # instant / queue.push((k, v)) / # flusher writes queue to DB every 5s
column6: Write-through — through waits for the store before acking; behind acks first and gambles on the flush.

column3: Every cache entry parks at its own meter. When the meter hits zero the tow truck hauls the data away, however shiny the car — freshness by countdown, no judgment involved.
column4: Each entry carries a time-to-live; past it the entry counts as gone, bounding staleness without any invalidation logic.
column5: SET price:sku42 '9.99' EX 60 / -- worst case: 60s stale / no purge code needed when the price changes
column6: LRU eviction — eviction reacts to capacity pressure; TTL removes by age even in a half-empty cache.

column3: You change your phone number, then must hunt down every place the old one lives: friends' phones, forms, the fridge magnet, grandma's book. Miss one and someone confidently dials the wrong number for years — a stale cache.
column4: Purging or updating every cached copy exactly when the source changes is notoriously error-prone — one of the two hard things in CS.
column5: UPDATE products SET name='X2' WHERE id=42; / copies: Redis, CDN, materialized view, browser / purge all, in order, race-free -- or serve lies
column6: TTL expiry — TTL is the blunt workaround that accepts bounded staleness; invalidation is the precise, hard, event-driven purge.

column3: A stuffed closet: LRU tosses whatever you wore longest ago; LFU counts wears and tosses the least-worn. The tux worn once last night survives LRU's purge but is first out under LFU.
column4: When full, the cache evicts by recency (LRU: least recently used) or by frequency (LFU: least frequently used) to make room.
column5: @functools.lru_cache(maxsize=1000) / Redis: maxmemory-policy allkeys-lru / (or allkeys-lfu for frequency)
column6: TTL — TTL removes entries because they are old; eviction removes them because the cache is full.

column3: The bakery's 'fresh until 9:00' sign flips and the whole queue charges the tiny kitchen at once. Smart baker: one runner fetches the new tray (lock) while everyone else gets yesterday's croissant (stale), and tomorrow's sign flips at 9:07 (jitter).
column4: When a hot key expires, many concurrent misses hammer the source at once; fix with per-key locks, TTL jitter, or serving stale while one refreshes.
column5: if cache.miss(k): / if lock.acquire(k): v = db.get(k); cache.set(k,v) / else: v = cache.get_stale(k) # or brief wait
column6: Ordinary cache miss — a stampede is thousands of simultaneous misses on one hot key, not a single cold read.

column3: The doorman keeps a pencil list of names NOT on the guest list. The same gatecrasher returns five times: five glances at the not-list, zero trips to the ledger inside. He erases it often — people do get invited eventually.
column4: Cache the fact that a lookup found nothing, so repeated misses for the same absent key stop hitting the store; keep its TTL short.
column5: u = cache.get('user:999') / if u == 'NOT_FOUND': return 404 # no DB hit / cache.set('user:999','NOT_FOUND', ttl=30)
column6: Regular caching — this stores absence, not values; too long a TTL makes newly created items look missing.

column3: IKEA logic: the assembled chair (object graph, pointers as glued joints) can't ship. Flatten it into a labeled box of parts (bytes) with instructions; the buyer rebuilds an identical chair in a different living room (process).
column4: Converting in-memory structures into a byte or text sequence for storage or transfer, and deserializing them back on the other side.
column5: data = json.dumps({'id': 7, 'tags': ['a']}) / send over network / write to disk / obj = json.loads(data) # other process or language
column6: Serializable isolation level — unrelated despite the name: that is transaction ordering, not encoding objects to bytes.

column3: Jason, the friendly courier every country understands: travels light, speaks plainly, checks no ID (schema). But he can't pronounce dates — he hands them over scribbled as strings — and drops any coin bigger than 2^53.
column4: Ubiquitous text format of objects, arrays, strings, numbers, booleans, null — human-readable and schema-free; no comments, dates, or safe ints past 2^53.
column5: {"id": 7, "tags": ["a", "b"], / "ts": "2026-07-10T12:00:00Z"} / -- the date is just a string by convention
column6: JavaScript object literal — JSON is stricter: double-quoted keys, no comments, no trailing commas, no functions.

column3: A poem whose meaning hangs on indentation — nudge one space and a stanza changes parents. In the last line the country code NO freezes into boolean false: Norway, voted out of existence by YAML 1.1.
column4: Indentation-structured, human-first format beloved for config; comments and anchors, but whitespace is syntax and unquoted scalars get coerced.
column5: server: / port: 8080 / country: NO # YAML 1.1 reads false; quote 'NO'
column6: JSON — YAML adds comments, anchors, multi-line strings; but JSON never turns NO into false or breaks on a stray space.

column3: Data in full Victorian dress: every value is announced on arrival AND departure — <name>Ada</name> — chaperoned by namespaces and corseted by a schema. Ceremonious and heavy, but nobody sneaks in unvalidated.
column4: Tag-based markup with attributes, namespaces and XSD validation — verbose, strict about well-formedness, still core to enterprise and documents.
column5: <order id="7"> / <item sku="A1" qty="2"/> / </order> validated against an XSD
column6: HTML — HTML is forgiving display markup for browsers; XML is strict data markup that dies on one unclosed tag.

column3: A military telegram in dense number code: 'field 1: 7, field 3: Ada' — no names on the wire, just numbered slots. Both ends drill from the same codebook (.proto); lose the codebook and the bytes are gibberish.
column4: Binary format with a compiled .proto schema; fields travel as numbers, not names — tiny, fast, typed, with codegen per language.
column5: message User { / int64 id = 1; / string name = 2; } // wire: tag numbers + values
column6: Avro — Avro ships or registers the schema with the data; protobuf assumes both sides already compiled the codebook.

column3: A shipping container with the packing manifest riveted to its door: any dock, even one that has never seen this shipper, unloads it by reading the attached schema; old docks reconcile new manifests line by line (schema resolution).
column4: Binary row format whose schema travels with the data (file header or registry ID), enabling clean schema resolution between versions.
column5: Kafka + Schema Registry: / record bytes start with schema id 42 / reader fetches schema 42, resolves vs its own
column6: Protobuf — protobuf's schema is compiled into both ends and absent from the wire; Avro's schema accompanies the data.

column3: A parquet floor laid in long strips — each board strip is one column running the whole room. Refinishing the 'price' strip never touches the other boards, and identical boards in a strip compress into one stamped plank.
column4: Columnar file format: each column's values stored contiguously with compression and statistics, so scans read only the columns they need.
column5: df.write.parquet('s3://sales/') / SELECT AVG(amount) FROM sales / -- reads only 'amount' column chunks + stats
column6: Avro — Avro is row-oriented, ideal for streaming whole records; Parquet is columnar, ideal for scanning few columns of many rows.

column3: Cassette decks across generations: your new deck still plays grandma's old tapes (backward); her old deck plays your new mixtape by skipping tracks it doesn't recognize (forward). House rule: add tracks with defaults, never reuse a track number.
column4: Changing a serialized schema while old and new programs interoperate: backward = new reader reads old data; forward = old reader reads new data.
column5: safe: add optional field with a default / unsafe: rename, retype, or reuse field id 3 / registry enforces BACKWARD / FORWARD / FULL
column6: Database schema migration — that mutates live tables with DDL; evolution keeps readers and writers of encoded records compatible.

column3: Gulliver's Lilliputians wage war over which end of the egg to crack first. Your 4-byte integer sails between their shores: 0x01020304 lands as 04 03 02 01 on the little-endian beach — same egg, opposite crack.
column4: Byte order for multi-byte numbers: big-endian stores the most significant byte first, little-endian the least; mismatches scramble binary data.
column5: 0x01020304 -> bytes: / big-endian: 01 02 03 04 (network order) / little-endian: 04 03 02 01 (x86, most ARM)
column6: Character encoding (UTF-8) — encoding maps characters to bytes; endianness orders the bytes within one numeric value.

column3: Two grenades hide in every payload: a clock and a coin. The clock stamped 01/02/03 explodes into three different days on three continents; the coin dropped into float acid dissolves to 0.30000000000000004. Defuse with ISO 8601 UTC and integer cents.
column4: Serialize instants as ISO 8601 UTC (or epoch), never ambiguous local formats; never put money in binary floats — use integer cents or decimals.
column6: Storing local wall-clock time — right for future human events (meetings follow local rules); past instants belong in UTC.

column3: This library never lends a sentence — you must check out the whole 8KB pamphlet even to read one line. Every cart, shelf, and reading desk (buffer pool) moves pamphlets, never loose sentences (rows).
column4: The fixed-size block (commonly 8KB) that engines read, write, cache, and lock; rows live inside pages and all I/O moves whole pages.
column5: Postgres default page: 8KB / reading one 40-byte row still does 8KB of I/O / pages are the buffer-pool and WAL-image unit too
column6: OS memory page (4KB) — same idea one layer down; the engine's page is its own on-disk and buffer-pool unit.

column3: A banyan tree pruned absurdly wide and shallow: trunk to any of a billion leaves in three or four hops. Repairs are carved directly into the leaf where the fruit hangs (in-place update), keeping the whole tree forever sorted.
column4: Keeps rows in a balanced, very wide tree of sorted pages; point reads and updates edit pages in place — read-optimized, the mature default.
column5: MySQL InnoDB, Postgres B-tree indexes / height ~3-4 levels for billions of keys / point read = one root-to-leaf descent
column6: Binary search tree — one key per node and towering height; B-tree nodes pack hundreds of keys so the tree stays squat and disk-friendly.

column3: A chef's order spike: new tickets stab on instantly (memtable — fast writes). A full spike is frozen and filed as a sorted stack (SSTable flush); finding an old order means rummaging several stacks until the night porter merges them (compaction).
column4: Buffers writes in a memtable, flushes sorted immutable files, merges them in background — random writes become sequential appends; write-optimized.
column5: RocksDB, Cassandra, LevelDB / write: append WAL + memtable insert (fast) / read: memtable, then newest-to-oldest SSTables
column6: B-tree engine — B-trees update pages in place, favoring reads; LSM appends and merges, favoring write throughput at read cost.

column3: The captain's iron rule: write the maneuver in the logbook before touching the sails. When the storm (crash) hits mid-turn, the surviving mate replays the logbook line by line and the ship ends exactly where the entries promised.
column4: Every change is appended and fsynced to a sequential log before data pages are touched; replaying the log after a crash restores committed work.
column5: COMMIT = WAL record fsynced (sequential, fast) / data pages updated lazily later / crash -> replay WAL from last checkpoint
column6: Audit trail — the WAL is physical, engine-internal, recycled after checkpoints; an audit trail is business-level and kept for humans.

column3: Each flush freezes a mini-dictionary in perfect alphabetical order. Nobody writes in a frozen book — corrections appear in a newer volume that shadows the old entry, and a doorman (bloom filter) swears which volumes definitely lack your word.
column4: Immutable files of sorted key-value pairs flushed from the memtable; served via sparse indexes and bloom filters, never edited — only superseded.
column5: flush memtable -> users-000123.sst (sorted, frozen) / bloom filter: 'definitely absent' for cheap / sparse index -> one seek into the file
column6: Memtable — the mutable in-RAM stage; SSTables are its frozen, sorted, on-disk descendants.

column3: A Zamboni for the dictionary stacks: between periods it glides over ten scratched-up frozen volumes, merges them into one smooth sheet, and scrapes the dead entries (tombstones) off as ice shavings.
column4: Background merge of overlapping SSTables into fewer files, keeping newest versions and dropping tombstoned deletes — pays I/O now for faster reads later.
column5: 10 SSTables, key x appears 3 times -> / compact to 1 file: newest x kept, tombstones gone / fewer files = fewer seeks per read
column6: VACUUM (Postgres) — vacuum reclaims dead MVCC row versions in mutable heaps; compaction merges immutable LSM files.

column3: A museum that hands each visitor time-stamped photocopies: you tour the collection exactly as it looked when you entered, while artists repaint originals in the same halls. Nobody waits; a janitor (VACUUM) later shreds copies no visitor can still see.
column4: Keeps multiple versions of each row; every transaction reads a consistent snapshot, so readers never block writers and writers never block readers.
column5: Postgres: UPDATE writes a new row version (xmin/xmax) / older snapshots still see the prior version / VACUUM reclaims versions no txn can see
column6: Lock-based concurrency — locking makes readers and writers queue; MVCC gives readers snapshots so they never queue behind writers.

column3: The librarian keeps the most-asked-for pamphlets heaped on her front desk; regulars never see the stacks. Pencil edits made on desk copies (dirty pages) are walked back to the shelves on periodic rounds (checkpoints).
column4: The engine's RAM cache of hot pages: reads hit memory instead of disk, and dirty pages are flushed back at checkpoints; hit ratio rules performance.
column5: Postgres shared_buffers, InnoDB buffer pool / 99% hit ratio: most reads never touch disk / dirty pages flushed at checkpoint
column6: Query result cache — that stores final answers to whole queries; the buffer pool caches raw pages that every query shares.

column3: A record needle gliding along one groove pours out music (sequential); the DJ lifting and dropping the arm across tracks (random) buys a silent second per jump. The WAL and LSM exist to keep the needle in the groove.
column4: Contiguous access vastly outruns scattered seeks — brutal on HDDs, still real on SSDs — so engines turn random writes into sequential logs and appends.
column5: HDD: ~150 MB/s sequential vs ~100 IOPS random / SSD: gap narrows but sequential still wins / (prefetch, erase blocks, queue depth)
column6: Throughput vs latency in general — this is specifically about access pattern: the same device is orders faster when access is ordered.

column3: 'It is written' means nothing until the wax seal: fsync presses the ring into hot wax and waits for it to harden. Skip it and your letter was merely spoken to the mail clerk (OS page cache), who may not survive the night.
column4: Forces the OS to flush its buffered writes for a file down to durable media before returning; without it, written data can vanish on power loss.
column5: f.write(data) # app buffer / f.flush() # to OS cache / os.fsync(f.fileno()) # to disk -- durable
column6: flush() — flush moves data from app buffers into the OS cache; only fsync forces the OS cache onto durable media.

column3: Downstairs, checkout lanes beep thousands of tiny basket updates a minute (OLTP). Upstairs at midnight, one accountant reads EVERY receipt of the year to ask how bananas did (OLAP). Different rooms, different filing.
column4: OLTP: many tiny concurrent reads/writes touching single rows (row stores). OLAP: few huge scans aggregating millions of rows (column stores).
column5: OLTP: UPDATE cart SET qty=2 WHERE id=9; / OLAP: SELECT region, SUM(rev) FROM sales_5y / GROUP BY region;
column6: HTAP — hybrid engines try both in one system; the classic split is row store for OLTP, columnar warehouse for OLAP.

column3: Airport customs before entry: luggage is pulled off the plane (extract), opened, inspected and repacked in the customs hall (transform), and only cleared bags roll into the country — the warehouse (load). Nothing dirty crosses the border.
column4: Extract from sources, transform (clean, conform, join) in a processing layer, then load the polished result into the warehouse.
column5: nightly: pull Postgres + CSVs (E) / Spark cleans, dedupes, conforms (T) / load dim/fact tables into warehouse (L)
column6: ELT — the letters swap: ELT loads raw data first and transforms inside the warehouse with SQL.

column3: Moving day: the truck dumps every box straight into the garage (load raw). You unpack inside at leisure with the house's own tools (SQL transforms) — and next year you can re-unpack differently, because the original boxes are still there.
column4: Load raw data straight into the warehouse, then transform it there with SQL (dbt et al.); cheap storage and elastic compute made raw-first practical.
column5: Fivetran/Airbyte copy raw tables to Snowflake / dbt models: staging -> marts, all in SQL / re-run anytime; the raw layer is untouched
column6: ETL — ETL transforms before loading, so raw data never lands; ELT keeps raw data queryable and re-transformable.

column3: The hamper fills all week; Sunday's one big wash handles everything at once — cheap per sock, and a ruined load just gets washed again (rerun). But Tuesday's mustard stain sits there until Sunday (latency).
column4: Process accumulated data in scheduled bounded chunks; high throughput and simple retries, at the cost of latency until the next run.
column5: 02:00 cron: spark-submit daily_job.py / processes yesterday's partition ds=2026-07-09 / failure? rerun the whole day idempotently
column6: Stream processing — streams handle each event on arrival (seconds); batch waits for the scheduled window (hours).

column3: A sushi conveyor: each plate is handled the instant it glides past — nothing piles up. The chef groups plates into five-minute windows and holds each window open a grace period for plates stuck behind a slow customer (watermark).
column4: Continuously process unbounded event flows as they arrive, using windows, state, and watermarks for late data; low latency, higher complexity.
column5: Kafka -> Flink job scores each txn in <1s / window: 5 min tumbling, watermark 30s late / state lives inside the stream processor
column6: Message queue — a queue only delivers events; stream processing computes over the flow with windows, joins, and state.

column3: A museum, not a storage unit: every exhibit was cleaned, verified and labeled before display (schema-on-write); visitors (analysts) wander the curated halls asking anything. Nothing enters uncatalogued.
column4: Central analytics store of cleaned, modeled, schema-enforced tables (facts and dimensions), columnar underneath, built for fast SQL aggregation.
column5: Snowflake / BigQuery / Redshift / analysts: SELECT ... FROM fact_sales JOIN dim_* / fed by ETL/ELT pipelines
column6: Data lake — the lake stores raw files of any shape; the warehouse stores curated, typed, query-ready tables.

column3: A reservoir: raw water pours in from every stream untested — logs, CSVs, images. Anyone may dip a bucket, but each drinker filters at the shore (schema-on-read). Fire the park rangers (catalog, governance) and it silts into a swamp.
column4: Cheap object storage holding raw files in any format, schema applied on read; flexible and vast — ungoverned, it degrades into a data swamp.
column5: s3://lake/raw/events/2026/07/10/*.json.gz / Athena/Spark apply schema at query time / catalog (Glue/Unity) or nobody finds anything
column6: Lakehouse — adds table formats with ACID and schema (Iceberg, Delta) atop lake files, blending warehouse behavior into the lake.

column3: Ask a full stadium the average age: the column store passes down one thin ribbon listing only ages — similar numbers that zip together tightly. The row store instead hands you every fan's entire wallet, ticket stubs and all.
column4: Analytics reads touch only the queried columns, and same-typed neighboring values compress hard — often ~100x less I/O than row storage.
column5: 1B rows x 50 cols, query touches 1 col: / columnar reads ~2% of bytes, then compresses / row store drags all 50 columns per row
column6: Wide-column store (Cassandra) — a row-oriented OLTP design despite the name; columnar is a physical layout for scan speed.

column3: An ice-cube tray for events: each day freezes into its own cube. Asking about Tuesday pops out one cube — nobody thaws the whole freezer (full scan). Retention is snapping off a stale cube, not chiseling the block.
column4: Split a table or dataset into parts by a key (usually date) so queries prune to relevant partitions and old data can be dropped wholesale.
column5: CREATE TABLE events (...) PARTITION BY RANGE (ds); / WHERE ds='2026-07-09' -- scans 1 of 365 / DROP PARTITION for retention: instant
column6: Sharding — sharding spreads data across machines for write scale; partitioning splits within one dataset for pruning and lifecycle.

column3: A rubber stamp, not a tally pen: stamping the same page five times leaves one clean mark. The intern with the tally pen re-counts on every rerun, and Monday's revenue doubles each time the job hiccups.
column4: Design jobs so reruns produce the same final state — overwrite the target partition, dedupe by key — making retries and backfills safe.
column5: INSERT OVERWRITE TABLE sales PARTITION (ds='2026-07-09') / run twice -> same rows, no double counting / (vs INSERT INTO: each rerun duplicates)
column6: Exactly-once delivery — a transport guarantee; idempotence makes at-least-once delivery safe by construction, the practical path.

column3: App validators are polite greeters at the front door, easily bypassed via the side entrance (admin script, 2 a.m. psql). The constraint is the vault's steel door in the only corridor — every path funnels through it, and it never sleeps.
column4: Database-enforced rules catch bad data from every path — app bugs, cron jobs, manual SQL; app validation is UX, the constraint is the guarantee.
column5: Rails validates :email, presence: true # skippable / update_all, raw SQL, other services bypass it / DB UNIQUE/NOT NULL/FK/CHECK cannot be bypassed
column6: Application validation — friendlier errors, but only on paths that run it; a constraint binds every writer of the table.

column3: A paper form with a mousetrap under one box: leave it blank and SNAP — the whole form (row) is rejected at the counter. No half-filled forms ever enter the archive.
column4: Declares that a column can never hold NULL, so every row must supply (or default) a value; the cheapest data-quality win there is.
column5: email TEXT NOT NULL / INSERT INTO users(name) VALUES ('Ada'); / ERROR: null value violates not-null constraint
column6: DEFAULT — a default fills in a missing value at insert; NOT NULL also rejects an explicit NULL.

column3: The marathon official at the start line scans bib numbers against a sorted roster (unique index): a second runner in bib 1042 is yanked off the course before the gun — no two racers ever share a number mid-race.
column4: Guarantees no two rows share the same value(s) in the constrained column(s), enforced by a unique index; NULLs typically don't count as duplicates.
column5: ALTER TABLE users ADD CONSTRAINT uq_email UNIQUE (email); / second signup with the same email: / ERROR: duplicate key value violates uq_email
column6: Primary key — a PK is UNIQUE plus NOT NULL and one per table; UNIQUE constraints can be many and usually admit NULLs.

column3: The amusement-ride height stick bolted at the gate: 'you must be price >= 0 to ride'. The machine measures every row at the turnstile — no operator judgment, no exceptions, not even for staff (admin scripts).
column4: A declarative boolean expression evaluated on every insert or update; rows failing the check are rejected by the engine itself.
column5: ALTER TABLE products / ADD CONSTRAINT positive CHECK (price >= 0); / UPDATE products SET price=-5; -- check violation
column6: Trigger — triggers run arbitrary code and can see other rows; CHECK is a simple per-row predicate the engine fully understands.

column3: Demolition day at the parent building: CASCADE flattens every tenant apartment with it; SET NULL leaves tenants standing in the street with no address on file; RESTRICT — the crane refuses to swing while anyone still lives there.
column4: ON DELETE rules decide the children's fate when a parent row dies: CASCADE deletes them too, SET NULL blanks the link, RESTRICT blocks the delete.
column5: user_id BIGINT REFERENCES users(id) / ON DELETE CASCADE / DELETE FROM users WHERE id=7; -- orders go too
column6: Foreign key concept (702) — that is the reference itself; cascade actions are the enforced reaction when the referenced row disappears.

column3: The database carries a passport: every schema change is a numbered stamp on the next page. A fresh database replays every stamp in order and arrives at today; a hand-edit without a stamp creates a state no one can reproduce.
column4: Versioned, ordered scripts that change the database schema in lockstep with code; every environment replays the same numbered steps to the same state.
column5: migrations/0042_add_total_to_orders.sql / tools: Flyway, Alembic, Rails, Liquibase / applied once, recorded in a schema_version table
column6: Serialized-format schema evolution (767) — that keeps encoded records readable across versions; migration rewrites live tables with DDL.

column3: Replacing a bridge without closing the road: build the new span alongside (expand), let traffic use both while repainting the lanes (dual-write, backfill), and demolish the old span only when the last car is off it (contract).
column4: Zero-downtime schema change: add the new shape (expand), dual-write and backfill, switch reads, then drop the old (contract); each step suits both versions.
column5: 1) ADD COLUMN full_name / 2) code writes both; backfill old rows / 3) switch reads; 4) DROP first_name, last_name
column6: Blue-green deployment — swaps whole app environments; expand-contract evolves one shared database both versions must use.

column3: The extinguisher gleaming on the wall is your nightly dump; the fire drill is the restore. GitLab 2017: five backup mechanisms, zero restorable when production vanished. Until you rehearse, the backup is both alive and dead — Schrödinger's backup.
column4: A backup only exists once a restore has been rehearsed: regularly restore to a scratch environment and verify, or you own Schrödinger's backup.
column5: weekly job: restore latest dump to staging / run row counts + app smoke tests / alert if restore time exceeds RTO
column6: Replication — replicas copy your DROP TABLE within milliseconds; only point-in-time backups let you return to before the mistake.

column3: Instead of ripping the seat out, the theater drapes a 'reserved — do not sell' cloth over it. Auditors may lift the cloth (history intact), but every usher, forever, must remember to skip cloaked seats — one forgetful query sells a ghost a ticket.
column4: Mark rows deleted (a deleted_at flag) instead of removing them, preserving history and undo — at the price of filtering every query forever.
column5: UPDATE users SET deleted_at = now() WHERE id=7; / every query: WHERE deleted_at IS NULL / (or hide behind a view / default scope)
column6: Archiving to a history table — moves rows out, keeping the live table clean; soft delete leaves flagged rows in every query's path.

column3: A guestbook chained beside every exhibit: each touch writes a line in ink — who, what, when, old value, new value. The pen has no eraser, the chain has no key, and the curator's own meddling is logged like everyone else's.
column4: An append-only record of who changed what, when, and from/to which values — for compliance, debugging, and trust; nobody edits it, not even admins.
column5: audit_log(id, table_name, row_id, actor, / action, old_val, new_val, at) / INSERT-only; written by trigger or app layer
column6: Write-ahead log — the WAL is physical, recycled after checkpoints, for crash recovery; the audit trail is logical, permanent, for humans.
